findings.claim: On the 12-mark Discuss, examiners reward students who present the views of at least two named sociologists or perspectives and reach a supported conclusion. One-sided answers that only present the interactionist view, for example, cannot reach the Mastering tier.
findings.truth: A fabricated statement about what examiners reward. The spec (assessment section, lines 299-325) sets Paper 2 Section A as two multiple-choice questions plus short and extended responses; it publishes no such examiner instruction. The advice itself (two perspectives plus a supported judgement) is sound, so state it as advice, not as an examiner claim.
findings.evidence: spec 'Paper 2' assessment section; house rule on fabricated examiner claims and mark-scheme wording

findings.claim: Cannabis possession is legal for recreational use in the Netherlands under certain conditions but remains a criminal offence in England and Wales.
findings.truth: Recreational cannabis is not legal in the Netherlands. Possession, use and trade stay illegal under Dutch law; a formal tolerance policy (gedoogbeleid) tells prosecutors not to prosecute possession of up to five grams. The cross-place point needs a country where the act really is legal (Canada legalised recreational cannabis in 2018).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Drug policy of the Netherlands (fetched 6 Sep 2026): 'technically illegal under Dutch law', 'possession of a maximum amount of five grams cannabis for personal use is not prosecuted'

findings.claim: Cannabis possession is permitted under certain conditions in the Netherlands but is a criminal offence in England and Wales.
findings.truth: Same error as F2 in the flashcard answer: Dutch cannabis possession is illegal but tolerated, not permitted. Replace with a country where recreational possession is legal.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Drug policy of the Netherlands (fetched 6 Sep 2026)

findings.claim: Police-recorded crime and self-report studies both suggest that working-class individuals are overrepresented in offending data, particularly for street crime, theft and burglary.
findings.truth: Self-report studies do the opposite: they show offending spread far more evenly across social classes than police-recorded crime implies. Lesson 7 of this same unit states this correctly ('Self-report studies have consistently shown that offending is far more widespread across social classes and ethnic groups than official statistics suggest'), so the unit contradicts itself. A student who cites self-report studies as evidence of working-class overrepresentation loses the point the spec asks for on the usefulness of crime data.
findings.evidence: spec 3.5.4 'Data on crime' (main sources, patterns and trends, the dark figure); internal contradiction with L7 content_html

findings.claim: New Right perspectives tend to favour tougher sentencing and longer prison terms as deterrents, arguing that lenient sentencing encourages a dependency culture in which offenders face insufficient consequences.
findings.truth: 'Dependency culture' is Murray's welfare concept: state benefits creating an underclass that does not work. It is not a claim about sentencing. The New Right argument on sentencing is deterrence and individual responsibility. Students meet Murray again in social stratification, so the muddle costs them there too.
findings.evidence: spec key thinkers section on Murray (underclass, illegitimacy, welfare dependency, rising crime rate)

findings.claim: Official figures consistently show that male offenders account for roughly three-quarters of all prosecutions.
findings.truth: Unsourced and probably low. Ministry of Justice 'Women and the criminal justice system' figures put the female share of prosecutions in the low-to-mid twenties per cent, so the male share is nearer four-fifths, and the female share is inflated by TV licence prosecutions. The claim is hedged ('roughly'), so it is not plainly wrong. Could not verify: both gov.uk statistics pages returned 404 and the WebSearch budget is spent.
findings.evidence: attempted WebFetch of gov.uk women-and-the-criminal-justice-system pages (404); no verified value found

findings.claim: Robert Merton, writing in Social Theory and Social Structure (1938, enlarged 1968)
findings.truth: The 1938 date belongs to Merton's article 'Social Structure and Anomie'; the book Social Theory and Social Structure appeared in 1949. The AQA spec prints exactly the same citation ('Merton R K, Social Theory and Social Structure, New York, The Free Press, 1938 (republished in an enlarged edition in 1968)'), so the lesson matches the authority a student and a marker will use. Leave it.

findings.claim: Heidensohn noted that the criminal justice system has historically applied labels differently to men and women: women offenders are sometimes treated more leniently (the 'chivalry thesis') when they conform to feminine stereotypes
findings.truth: The chivalry thesis is Pollak's (1950). Heidensohn discussed and criticised it and is associated with the double-deviance argument, so 'noted' is defensible and no authorship is claimed. The spec's Heidensohn entry is only about control theory and female conformity, so the drift is worth watching but not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: spec key thinkers 7.3, Heidensohn entry (control theory, patriarchal control in home, public and work)

findings.claim: Every 12-mark mark scheme in the unit (L1-L7) and five exam tips (L1, L2, L4, L5, L6, L7) grade answers on a Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging ladder.
findings.truth: That ladder is invented: AQA does not use those band names, and the house vocabulary is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. Two options: (a) relabel all seven mark schemes and the exam-tip references now, or (b) leave the unit to the programme's band-ladder workstream, which is already sizing 178 ladders. Recommendation: (b) leave it, so all units get one consistent relabel; F1 removes one 'Mastering tier' reference only because the fabricated examiner claim in the same sentence had to go.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright-distancing section; spec assessment section (no published band names for GCSE Sociology in the spec)
findings.ruling: NOTE: Mastering/Secure/Developing/Emerging ladder left for the programme-wide band-ladder relabel sweep.

summary: Sociologist attributions, dates and studies are sound throughout (Durkheim, Merton's five adaptations, Albert Cohen 1955, Becker 1963, Stanley Cohen 1972 Clacton, Heidensohn 1985, Carlen 1988 with 39 women), all 35 knowledge-check keys are correct, and every practice question sits on the 1/2/3/4/12 ladder with no invented paper or timing claims. Five fixes: one fabricated examiner claim, a wrong legal status for cannabis in the Netherlands (twice), self-report studies cited as evidence of working-class overrepresentation (contradicting L7), and 'dependency culture' misapplied to sentencing.
